extraction.body: Eight intermediate certificates issued by Indian certificate authority eMudhra were secured with private keys so weak that anyone could recover them from the public certificates in under a second. On its website, the company highlights that it has issued more than 60 million digital certificates. A security researcher known as Wayne discovered the flaw on October 17 while running a check against the Common CA Database (CCADB). To prove the keys were compromised, he signed the message “We have a problem here – Wayne” with each of them and sent his report to Apple, Google, Microsoft, Mozilla and eMudhra. Mozilla’s Dennis Jackson made the incident public on October 20 in a statement on the organization’s dev-security-policy forum, warning that the keys could let attackers issue fraudulent HTTPS certificates for websites they don’t control. The certificates chain to roots trusted by Apple, Google, Microsoft and Mozilla. “This is a serious security incident with implications across the Internet,” stated Cloudflare. “These certificates were widely trusted by browsers, operating systems, and also within Cloudflare. Because the keys themselves are weak, an attacker can create a forged certificate for any domain and use it to impersonate servers to intercept or modify traffic,” the company added . According to Mozilla’s incident report, the eight affected keys came from a batch of 24 intermediates eMudhra generated on April 30, 2025. Six issue TLS certificates for websites and two are used for code signing, and certificate authority Sectigo cross-signed all eight in May 2025. A private key of this type is meant to be a random number more than 100 digits long. Each of these was smaller than 256, so anyone can find one by testing at most 256 values. Security researcher Scott Helme was among those who recovered the keys. “One of eMudhra’s certificate authority private keys is the number 4. Not a number that starts with 4, or the number 4 followed by a few hundred random digits, just, 4… Another one is 56, and another is 115. I know, because I recovered all of them from their public certificates on my laptop just now, and it took less than a second,” wrote Helme. “Normally when a CA key is compromised, someone stole it! There’s a thief, there’s a moment it happened, and you can at least reason about who now has access to that key.” “Here, nobody had to steal anything. The key was effectively public from the day the certificate existed,” added Helme. Chrome and Firefox blocked the certificates on the day of the report, Apple followed on October 19 and Microsoft on October 20. eMudhra revoked them on October 18. The flaw is so easy to exploit that, in Jackson’s words, “the impact of this incident could not be higher.” His concern lies with devices and applications that have no reliable way to learn that a certificate was revoked. After several people recovered the keys on their own and some said so publicly, Mozilla removed trust in the eMudhra root certificate that signed the intermediates. Google will do the same in Chrome and is “conducting a thorough evaluation regarding the status of eMudhra’s remaining CA certificate,” according to its Chrome Root Program. eMudhra has stopped issuing from that root and estimates that about 30,000 customer certificates need to be replaced. Responding on Mozilla’s bug tracker, eMudhra traced the problem to a faulty script used during the April 2025 key ceremony. The script created a second set of weaker keys, and because their labels resembled those of the properly generated keys, staff picked the weak ones when preparing the certificates. The company said only one of the intermediates was ever put into production and that none of them were used to issue certificates to customers. It admitted to human errors at several steps of the process and plans to re-check every key ceremony it has carried out. It is not known whether anyone recovered and used the weak keys in the 17 months before the flaw was reported. Browsers are protected, but apps, servers and devices that don’t receive revocation updates may still trust the certificates, Helme warned, which could expose user data to anyone able to intercept their traffic. The disclosure site set up by Jackson advises users to update their browsers and operating systems, and Helme recommends that administrators update the certificate lists their systems rely on.

sources.title: We can do impossible things - MIT Technology Review
passages: My brain, throughout my 20-plus-year career as a science and tech journalist, has played host to a near ­constant tug-of-war between ambition and reality.
Learning to find that balance is a big part of what’s helped me survive in this industry and, ultimately, led me here.
This past spring, I had the great privilege of joining the incredible team of journalists behind MIT Technology Review to take the reins of the print magazine.
They might say it’s as implausible as an AI kill switch, practical nuclear fusion, or a superconductor that works at room temperature.

But if I learned nothing else from three years spent finding ways for li’l old me (or li’l old you!) to chip away at one of humanity’s biggest existential threats, it’s that focusing on what we can’t do only makes the darkness darker.

extraction.body: It’s all too easy to lose sight of ambition when we’re busy playing whack-a-mole with the world’s problems. I’d wager everyone has a rehearsed response to what’s absolutely one of the world’s worst interview questions: “What’s your biggest weakness?” Whenever I’ve gotten it, I take a slow—even pensive—breath and rattle off my line: “I say no to myself too much.” I won’t lie. It’s a bit shameless—a definite humblebrag. I’m a systems thinker: When an idea pops up, I immediately spin up a feasibility assessment in my head. I run lists, plot timelines, and tally budget line items. Sometimes a rough Gantt chart starts to take shape. (I’m a gas at parties, as you can surely tell.) My brain, throughout my 20-plus-year career as a science and tech journalist, has played host to a near ­constant tug-of-war between ambition and reality. Learning to find that balance is a big part of what’s helped me survive in this industry and, ultimately, led me here. This past spring, I had the great privilege of joining the incredible team of journalists behind MIT Technology Review to take the reins of the print magazine. If you’ve been reading along with us for the last handful of issues, you may have noticed a few changes starting to materialize. We’ve brought back a regular roster of lists and infographics (both things that magazines do particularly well). But the biggest change is only just beginning to take shape, which is why Mat Honan, our editor in chief, asked me to hop in to introduce myself—and the issue you’re holding in your hands right now. We’re giving ourselves permission to play around and experiment. To be a little … audacious. Because, practical though I may be, I do still have plenty of ideas. It’s just that I sometimes need a reminder to stop blocking myself and do the thing . That’s the spirit driving this issue in particular. We wanted to end 2026 with a slate of stories that check in on impossible ideas. Why? Because it’s frankly a lot of fun to dream about living on the moon or uploading our brains. Because losing sight of ambition is all too easy when it feels as if we’re playing whack-a-mole with the world’s problems. But also because the scientists and engineers who absolutely refuse to give up on even the most daring endeavors—like making synthetic blood or decoding animals’ speech—remind us what this whole technology thing is supposed to do to begin with. It’s supposed to take cutting-edge research and development and apply it to make life better, safer, healthier, even more joyful. And when we eff up and make things worse (see: forever chemicals, traffic deaths, and AI that encourages potentially dangerous user behavior), we’re supposed to dig back in, assess the damage, and find ways to fix what we’ve broken. Even when unraveling the mess might itself seem impossible. Right before I came to MIT Technology Review, I edited a newsletter about individual actions that can help address the climate crisis, which some would call—and have called—a fool’s errand, given the sheer scale of the problem. They might say it’s as implausible as an AI kill switch, practical nuclear fusion, or a superconductor that works at room temperature. But if I learned nothing else from three years spent finding ways for li’l old me (or li’l old you!) to chip away at one of humanity’s biggest existential threats, it’s that focusing on what we can’t do only makes the darkness darker. So yeah, this one’s for the folks who have the audacity to try, and who refuse to let anyone—themselves included—tell them no.

extraction.body: Both problems could result in large-scale attacks and require massive cleanup. The web is a bit of a hot mess today following the discovery of two severe vulnerabilities, according to security releases seen by Ars Technica . The first involves TLS certificates with extremely weak encryption that could affect everything from VPNs to IoT devices. The other is a severe PHP programming language vulnerability impacting CMS systems including WordPress and Drupal. Both problems could result in large-scale attacks and require massive cleanup jobs, security experts said. gPHP Foundation said on X that it's releasing security patches for two critical vulnerabilities rated 9.2 out of 10 on the severity scale. Ahead of the release today at 14:00 UTC (10AM ET), the group said that "PHP users are encouraged to prepare to update," adding that it will issue an "earlier release if details become public or active exploit evidence." The advisory follows a report showing video of a tool called PHP2Shell running code on web servers including the latest versions of WordPress, MediaWiki, Symphony, Drupal and other PHP-based sites. The security firm watchTowr claims it has confirmed the vulnerability and that it affects every version from PHP 5 (2004) onward. "According to an unverified report, the vulnerability would let an attacker run their own code on a server running PHP, potentially taking control of it," watchTowr's FAQ on the exploit states. Another company, Sansec, said it expects "mass attacks to start within 15 minutes of the release." With all this, web admins are likely scrambling to patch the issue, so some PHP-based websites could go down briefly while that happens. The other issue with TLS certificates is a whole other bag of excrement. An India-based firm called eMudhra said eight of its intermediate CA certificates have been compromised that "chain to roots trusted by Mozilla, Microsoft, Apple and Chrome root programs and by many downstream trust stores." The issue is that the private keys are weak and could let attackers forge credentials for a range of websites and apps. The compromised private key sizes ranged from three to eight bits, rather than the usual 384 bits. Specifically, the private keys used by eMudhra were 4, 56, 66, 115, 155, 156, 230 and 237, according to Hacker News and other reports. Those would allow anyone to recover them by testing just 256 possible numbers. The eMudhra certificates were widely trusted by hosts like Cloudflare, as well as browsers, operating systems, IoT (Internet of Things) and other devices that connect to the internet. Once they forge domain certificates, attackers can use those domains to impersonate servers and intercept traffic. Mozilla, Google and Apple have blocked the compromised certificates for their browsers. The web is a bit of a hot mess today following the discovery of two severe vulnerabilities, according to security releases seen by Ars Technica . The first involves TLS certificates with extremely weak encryption that could affect everything from VPNs to IoT devices. The other is a severe PHP programming language vulnerability impacting CMS systems including WordPress and Drupal. Both problems could result in large-scale attacks and require massive cleanup jobs, security experts said.

gPHP Foundation said on X that it's releasing security patches for two critical vulnerabilities rated 9.2 out of 10 on the severity scale. Ahead of the release today at 14:00 UTC (10AM ET), the group said that "PHP users are encouraged to prepare to update," adding that it will issue an "earlier release if details become public or active exploit evidence."

The advisory follows a report showing video of a tool called PHP2Shell running code on web servers including the latest versions of WordPress, MediaWiki, Symphony, Drupal and other PHP-based sites. The security firm watchTowr claims it has confirmed the vulnerability and that it affects every version from PHP 5 (2004) onward. "According to an unverified report, the vulnerability would let an attacker run their own code on a server running PHP, potentially taking control of it," watchTowr's FAQ on the exploit states.

Another company, Sansec, said it expects "mass attacks to start within 15 minutes of the release." With all this, web admins are likely scrambling to patch the issue, so some PHP-based websites could go down briefly while that happens.

passages: So Baikovitz dropped “Robotics” from the company’s name and pivoted to developing AI-powered computer-aided design (CAD) software instead.
The bet paid off, as Mach9 has racked up nearly 100 customers for the private beta of its software, and they’ve used it on more than 2,500 projects to date.
Mach9’s AI CAD system takes the survey data and creates a first draft of a plan, which engineers can then refine.

The startup is “giving them all of the tools to draw, remove, adjust vertices, assess the quality of the AI-generated model, so that they can put effectively their name behind the deliverable that they’re producing, because there is a lot of liability in this particular industry, and it requires licensed professionals that know what they’re looking at,” Baikovitz said.
Mach9 is one of a number of startups racing to modernize the planning-to-building pipeline for construction and infrastructure.

In August, a startup called CivilGrid raised $26 million to grow what it calls the “Google Maps for the underground.” Meanwhile, Blueprints AI , which uses AI to produce code-compliant, permit-ready architectural blueprints in just a few minutes, was among the top 200 companies in the Startup Battlefield competition at last week’s TechCrunch Disrupt.

This allows customers doing surveying and civil engineering work to “expand their own capacity and take on more types of work, bigger projects, and expand the reach of how reality-capture data can influence major infrastructure decisions,” Baikovitz said.

But better software could “improve our efficiency in delivering these big statewide transportation mapping initiatives,” he said.

extraction.body: When Alex Baikovitz co-founded Mach9 Robotics in 2021, his goal was to build a better, faster, and cheaper way for civil engineers to do visual inspections. The company aimed to cut through red tape and modernize the slow, outdated processes that bog down construction in the United States. Within a few years, Mach9 Robotics had built that hardware, but the effort led Baikovitz to a realization: hardware wasn’t the bottleneck. “We saw how tedious it was for civil engineering organizations to take data from these amazing laser scanners and image data capture systems and turn that into a usable survey,” he told TechCrunch in an interview, referring to a detailed map of a site that engineers use for design work. “The real pain was in their workflows,” he said, and “how to turn all the endless amounts of data that they’re able to collect into . . .information that people can use to make the best design and asset management decisions across the board.” So Baikovitz dropped “Robotics” from the company’s name and pivoted to developing AI-powered computer-aided design (CAD) software instead. The bet paid off, as Mach9 has racked up nearly 100 customers for the private beta of its software, and they’ve used it on more than 2,500 projects to date. That momentum helped Mach9 unlock new funding. On Wednesday, the startup announced a $34 million Series A funding round co-led by First Round Capital and Bessemer Venture Partners. Also throwing in were Prudence, an early-stage, New York-based firm that focuses on investing in AI software use cases for construction and real estate, and Quiet Capital, a VC firm already on the cap table. Mach9 is one of a number of startups racing to modernize the planning-to-building pipeline for construction and infrastructure. In August, a startup called CivilGrid raised $26 million to grow what it calls the “Google Maps for the underground.” Meanwhile, Blueprints AI , which uses AI to produce code-compliant, permit-ready architectural blueprints in just a few minutes, was among the top 200 companies in the Startup Battlefield competition at last week’s TechCrunch Disrupt. Baikovitz said Mach9 is focused on disrupting CAD software because it’s one of the slowest and most labor-intensive pieces of that overall pipeline. “It takes months to be able to deliver a project, and about a week per mile for someone to do manually in the legacy incumbent software that’s built by the Autodesk and Bentley Systems of the world,” he said. Mach9 says its software automates a lot of that work, making the process 10 times faster and dramatically reducing costs. This allows customers doing surveying and civil engineering work to “expand their own capacity and take on more types of work, bigger projects, and expand the reach of how reality-capture data can influence major infrastructure decisions,” Baikovitz said. Baikovitz said Mach9 developed and trained its own in-house AI models to reach the centimeter-accurate level that construction and infrastructure work requires. “That’s not something that a lot of off-the-shelf models are able to do or deliver at in any capacity,” he said. “A big part of what our development process has looked like since 2024 has been, how do we build the industry leading models that can turn imagery or these multimodal image and laser scan data sets into survey grade like geometry, like tracing out the curbs, the pavement striping, all of this exactly how our customers want it to be at the accuracies that the industry demands.” Mach9’s AI CAD system takes the survey data and creates a first draft of a plan, which engineers can then refine. The startup is “giving them all of the tools to draw, remove, adjust vertices, assess the quality of the AI-generated model, so that they can put effectively their name behind the deliverable that they’re producing, because there is a lot of liability in this particular industry, and it requires licensed professionals that know what they’re looking at,” Baikovitz said. As for the funding, Baikovitz said his startup will split it between improving the product, hiring industry experts, and scaling “all parts of our organization to keep up with where the market is taking us.” In retrospect, Baikovitz said he’s thankful that he initially went down the hardware path. It gave his startup something to pitch to potential customers, and it was largely those customers who told him they didn’t need better devices to capture data. “I’m not interested in getting this cheaper, lower-cost hardware,” he remembers one VP telling him. But better software could “improve our efficiency in delivering these big statewide transportation mapping initiatives,” he said. He added that such projects help make states that Mach9 has worked with, like Texas, “much more like safe [and] effective.” Sean O’Kane is a reporter who has spent a decade covering the rapidly-evolving business and technology of the transportation industry, including Tesla and the many startups chasing Elon Musk. Most recently, he was a reporter at Bloomberg News where he helped break stories about some of the most notorious EV SPAC flops. He previously worked at The Verge, where he also covered consumer technology, hosted many short- and long-form videos, performed product and editorial photography, and once nearly passed out in a Red Bull Air Race plane. extraction.body: When Alex Baikovitz co-founded Mach9 Robotics in 2021, his goal was to build a better, faster, and cheaper way for civil engineers to do visual inspections. The company aimed to cut through red tape and modernize the slow, outdated processes that bog down construction in the United States. Within a few years, Mach9 Robotics had built that hardware, but the effort led Baikovitz to a realization: hardware wasn’t the bottleneck. “We saw how tedious it was for civil engineering organizations to take data from these amazing laser scanners and image data capture systems and turn that into a usable survey,” he told TechCrunch in an interview, referring to a detailed map of a site that engineers use for design work. “The real pain was in their workflows,” he said, and “how to turn all the endless amounts of data that they’re able to collect into . . .information that people can use to make the best design and asset management decisions across the board.” So Baikovitz dropped “Robotics” from the company’s name and pivoted to developing AI-powered computer-aided design (CAD) software instead. The bet paid off, as Mach9 has racked up nearly 100 customers for the private beta of its software, and they’ve used it on more than 2,500 projects to date. That momentum helped Mach9 unlock new funding. On Wednesday, the startup announced a $34 million Series A funding round co-led by First Round Capital and Bessemer Venture Partners. Also throwing in were Prudence, an early-stage, New York-based firm that focuses on investing in AI software use cases for construction and real estate, and Quiet Capital, a VC firm already on the cap table. Mach9 is one of a number of startups racing to modernize the planning-to-building pipeline for construction and infrastructure. In August, a startup called CivilGrid raised $26 million to grow what it calls the “Google Maps for the underground.” Meanwhile, Blueprints AI , which uses AI to produce code-compliant, permit-ready architectural blueprints in just a few minutes, was among the top 200 companies in the Startup Battlefield competition at last week’s TechCrunch Disrupt. Baikovitz said Mach9 is focused on disrupting CAD software because it’s one of the slowest and most labor-intensive pieces of that overall pipeline. “It takes months to be able to deliver a project, and about a week per mile for someone to do manually in the legacy incumbent software that’s built by the Autodesk and Bentley Systems of the world,” he said. Mach9 says its software automates a lot of that work, making the process 10 times faster and dramatically reducing costs. This allows customers doing surveying and civil engineering work to “expand their own capacity and take on more types of work, bigger projects, and expand the reach of how reality-capture data can influence major infrastructure decisions,” Baikovitz said. Baikovitz said Mach9 developed and trained its own in-house AI models to reach the centimeter-accurate level that construction and infrastructure work requires. “That’s not something that a lot of off-the-shelf models are able to do or deliver at in any capacity,” he said. “A big part of what our development process has looked like since 2024 has been, how do we build the industry leading models that can turn imagery or these multimodal image and laser scan data sets into survey grade like geometry, like tracing out the curbs, the pavement striping, all of this exactly how our customers want it to be at the accuracies that the industry demands.” Mach9’s AI CAD system takes the survey data and creates a first draft of a plan, which engineers can then refine. The startup is “giving them all of the tools to draw, remove, adjust vertices, assess the quality of the AI-generated model, so that they can put effectively their name behind the deliverable that they’re producing, because there is a lot of liability in this particular industry, and it requires licensed professionals that know what they’re looking at,” Baikovitz said. As for the funding, Baikovitz said his startup will split it between improving the product, hiring industry experts, and scaling “all parts of our organization to keep up with where the market is taking us.” In retrospect, Baikovitz said he’s thankful that he initially went down the hardware path. It gave his startup something to pitch to potential customers, and it was largely those customers who told him they didn’t need better devices to capture data. “I’m not interested in getting this cheaper, lower-cost hardware,” he remembers one VP telling him. But better software could “improve our efficiency in delivering these big statewide transportation mapping initiatives,” he said. He added that such projects help make states that Mach9 has worked with, like Texas, “much more like safe [and] effective.” Sean O’Kane is a reporter who has spent a decade covering the rapidly-evolving business and technology of the transportation industry, including Tesla and the many startups chasing Elon Musk. Most recently, he was a reporter at Bloomberg News where he helped break stories about some of the most notorious EV SPAC flops. Baikovitz said Mach9 developed and trained its own in-house AI models to reach the centimeter-accurate level that construction and infrastructure work requires.

“That’s not something that a lot of off-the-shelf models are able to do or deliver at in any capacity,” he said. “A big part of what our development process has looked like since 2024 has been, how do we build the industry leading models that can turn imagery or these multimodal image and laser scan data sets into survey grade like geometry, like tracing out the curbs, the pavement striping, all of this exactly how our customers want it to be at the accuracies that the industry demands.”

Mach9’s AI CAD system takes the survey data and creates a first draft of a plan, which engineers can then refine. The startup is “giving them all of the tools to draw, remove, adjust vertices, assess the quality of the AI-generated model, so that they can put effectively their name behind the deliverable that they’re producing, because there is a lot of liability in this particular industry, and it requires licensed professionals that know what they’re looking at,” Baikovitz said.

As for the funding, Baikovitz said his startup will split it between improving the product, hiring industry experts, and scaling “all parts of our organization to keep up with where the market is taking us.”

In retrospect, Baikovitz said he’s thankful that he initially went down the hardware path. It gave his startup something to pitch to potential customers, and it was largely those customers who told him they didn’t need better devices to capture data.

“I’m not interested in getting this cheaper, lower-cost hardware,” he remembers one VP telling him. But better software could “improve our efficiency in delivering these big statewide transportation mapping initiatives,” he said. He added that such projects help make states that Mach9 has worked with, like Texas, “much more like safe [and] effective.”
